title: Compromise Infrastructure: DNS Server
summary: Instead of running their own name service, an adversary takes over a third-party DNS server, the system that answers lookups of names to addresses, and uses it to support operations. The parent technique covers compromising third-party assets generally; here the compromised asset is resolution itself. Because the server is trusted by its clients and often authoritative for other organisations, changing its records silently redirects traffic to attacker-controlled systems, which can feed credential collection, session theft, or malware delivery. Control of name resolution can also be combined with fraudulently obtained digital certificates so that redirected sessions still look legitimate, and it can allow the operator to prove ownership of a name to a cloud service and thereby seize an administrative account. Subdomains can be created pointing at hostile servers without the real owner ever being notified. Detection focuses on the DNS server's own configuration and change logs, mismatches between registry and authoritative answers, unexpected certificate issuance for affected names, and users reporting that a known site resolves to an unfamiliar address.

beginner.definition: A DNS server is the internet service that translates a website name into the number a computer uses to reach it. This sub-technique is about an attacker breaking into someone else's DNS server and changing the answers it gives. The parent technique covers compromising other people's infrastructure. Here the compromised asset is name resolution.
beginner.whyItMatters: Whoever controls DNS controls where users really go. Victims type the right address and land on a criminal copy of the site. Because the address stays correct, browsers show no warning. The server's owner may see nothing unusual, since the machine keeps running and answering requests.
howItWorks: The attacker gains access to a DNS server, often through weak credentials or an unpatched flaw.
They edit records so chosen names now point at systems they control.
They obtain a matching digital certificate so the fake site still shows a padlock.
Users are redirected without any visible warning, and their data goes to the attacker.
They may add new subdomains pointing at hostile hosts while leaving other records unchanged.
They may also use the control to claim a domain at a cloud service and take over accounts.
beginner.example: Think of a library's printed directory of phone numbers. Someone swaps a single page so one charity's number now rings a call centre that asks for card details. The directory looks the same, and the charity's real phone keeps working perfectly.
takeaways: DNS servers are high-value targets because they decide where traffic really goes.
Changes to name records should be logged, reviewed, and alerted on.
Mismatches between your records and what external resolvers return deserve investigation.

objectives: Explain how this sub-technique differs from the parent Compromise Infrastructure technique.
Describe how altered DNS records enable redirection and credential theft.
Identify the configuration and log evidence left on a compromised name server.
Distinguish malicious record changes from planned DNS maintenance.
Explain why fraudulent certificates make redirection hard for users to detect.
